title: Juicy Chicken Breast (No More Dry)
summary: A 15-minute brine plus a sear-and-steam finish keeps lean chicken breast tender. The high-protein staple for meal prep.
body:
Why this works

A short salt brine seasons the meat and helps it hold water; finishing covered on low heat cooks it gently so it stays juicy right up to 74°C.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 2 boneless skinless chicken breasts (~180g each)
  • 2 tsp kosher salt (for the brine)
  • 1 tbsp olive oil · squeeze of lemon
  • ½ tsp each garlic powder, paprika, black pepper

Method

  1. Quick brine. Dissolve salt in 2 cups cold water; submerge the breasts 15 min. Pat very dry.
  2. Even them out. Pound the thick end so each breast is an even thickness.
  3. Season & sear. Rub with oil and spices. Sear in a hot pan 3–4 min until golden.
  4. Flip & steam. Flip, drop heat to low, cover, and cook 6–8 min to 74°C internal.
  5. Rest & slice. Rest 5 min, slice against the grain, finish with lemon.
Lean tip
Dry-sear in a nonstick pan with no oil to cut fat further — the brine still keeps it moist.

Storage

Keeps 4 days refrigerated. Slice cold over salads or into wraps.

title: Garlic Shrimp & Wilted Greens
summary: Ten-minute skillet of plump shrimp and dark greens in garlic and lemon. Almost all protein, barely any fat.
body:
Why this works

Shrimp cook in two minutes, so everything else goes in first. A hot pan and a quick toss keep them snappy, not rubbery.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 340g raw shrimp, peeled & deveined
  • 1 tbsp olive oil · 4 garlic cloves, sliced
  • 1 large bunch spinach or chard
  • Pinch chili flakes · juice of ½ lemon · salt

Method

  1. Bloom garlic. Warm oil, garlic, and chili over medium until fragrant, 1 min.
  2. Wilt greens. Add the greens with a pinch of salt; toss until just wilted. Push to the side.
  3. Sear shrimp. Add shrimp in one layer; cook 1–2 min per side until pink and opaque.
  4. Finish. Squeeze lemon over, toss everything together, taste for salt.
Lean tip
Serve over cauliflower rice or as-is — it's a complete low-carb plate at ~230 cal.

title: Egg-White & Veggie Scramble
summary: Fluffy egg-white scramble loaded with vegetables. A 10-minute breakfast that's nearly fat-free and high in protein.
body:
Why this works

Egg whites overcook fast and turn rubbery. Cook the veg first, then add whites off the strongest heat and pull them while still glossy.

Ingredients (serves 1)

  • 6 egg whites (or ~180ml carton whites)
  • 1 tsp olive oil · handful spinach
  • ½ bell pepper, diced · 2 mushrooms, sliced
  • Salt, pepper · pinch of chili or herbs

Method

  1. Soften veg. Sauté pepper and mushroom in the oil 3–4 min; add spinach to wilt.
  2. Add whites. Lower the heat. Pour in seasoned whites and let them set 20 sec.
  3. Fold gently. Push from the edges to the center in big folds until just set, ~1 min.
  4. Plate. Pull while glossy — carryover heat finishes them. Season and serve.
Lean tip
Add a tablespoon of feta or a slice of whole-grain toast if you want more without much fat.

title: Baked Cod with Burst Tomatoes
summary: Flaky cod roasted over garlicky cherry tomatoes. Lean white fish, hands-off oven time, big flavor.
body:
Why this works

Roasting the tomatoes first builds a quick pan sauce; the cod then bakes gently on top and stays just-set and flaky.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 2 cod fillets (~170g each)
  • 2 cups cherry tomatoes · 3 garlic cloves, smashed
  • 1 tbsp olive oil · pinch chili flakes
  • Salt, pepper · fresh basil or parsley · lemon

Method

  1. Preheat. Heat the oven to 220°C.
  2. Roast tomatoes. Toss tomatoes, garlic, oil, chili, salt on a tray; roast 12 min until bursting.
  3. Add the cod. Pat fillets dry, season, nestle into the tomatoes. Spoon some juices over.
  4. Bake. Roast 10–12 min until the fish flakes at 60°C.
  5. Finish. Squeeze lemon, scatter herbs, serve with the pan juices.
Lean tip
Any firm white fish works (haddock, pollock). Serve over greens to keep it low-carb.

title: Baked Turkey & Spinach Meatballs
summary: Lean ground-turkey meatballs bound with egg and spinach, baked not fried. Gluten-free and great for batch prep.
body:
Why this works

Lean turkey dries out easily; chopped spinach and an egg keep the meatballs moist, and baking on a rack lets fat drip away while they brown.

Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 500g lean ground turkey
  • 1 egg · 100g spinach, finely chopped
  • 3 garlic cloves, minced · 1 tsp each oregano, salt
  • 2 tbsp ground oats (optional binder) · black pepper

Method

  1. Preheat. Heat the oven to 200°C; line a tray (a rack helps).
  2. Mix. Combine turkey, egg, spinach, garlic, oats, and seasoning — don't overwork.
  3. Roll. Form ~16 even balls with damp hands.
  4. Bake. Bake 18–20 min until 74°C and lightly golden.
  5. Serve. Rest 2 min; serve with marinara, greens, or grains.
Lean tip
Use 99% lean turkey breast to drop the fat further; the spinach and egg still keep them tender.

Storage

Fridge 4 days; freezes well cooked. Reheat gently so they don't dry out.

title: Tuna & White Bean Salad
summary: A no-cook pantry lunch: canned tuna, creamy white beans, lemon and herbs. Ready in ten minutes, packed with protein and fiber.
body:
Why this works

Tuna packed in water keeps it lean; the beans add staying power and fiber. A bright lemon dressing ties it together — no cooking, no fuss.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 2 cans tuna in water, drained
  • 1 can white beans, rinsed
  • ¼ red onion, finely diced · handful parsley
  • Juice of 1 lemon · 1 tbsp olive oil · salt, pepper

Method

  1. Dress. Whisk lemon, oil, salt, and pepper in a bowl.
  2. Soften the onion. Stir the diced onion into the dressing; let it mellow 5 min.
  3. Combine. Fold in beans, flaked tuna, and parsley.
  4. Serve. Taste for lemon and salt; eat as-is or over greens.
Lean tip
Skip the oil and use extra lemon plus a spoon of the bean liquid for a near-fat-free dressing.

title: Chicken & Quinoa Power Bowl
summary: Seared chicken over fluffy quinoa with crisp veg and a lemon-tahini drizzle. A balanced, high-protein meal-prep bowl.
body:
Why this works

The quinoa simmers unattended while you cook the chicken and prep the veg, so the whole bowl comes together in one 30-minute window.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 2 chicken breasts (~180g each), cubed
  • ½ cup quinoa, rinsed · 1 cup water
  • 1 cucumber · 1 cup cherry tomatoes · handful greens
  • 2 tbsp tahini · juice of 1 lemon · 1 tsp olive oil · salt, cumin

Method

  1. Cook quinoa. Simmer quinoa in water, covered, ~15 min until fluffy; rest off heat.
  2. Sear chicken. Meanwhile, toss chicken with cumin and salt; sear in oil 6–8 min to 74°C.
  3. Prep veg. While both cook, dice cucumber and halve tomatoes.
  4. Whisk sauce. Stir tahini, lemon, and a splash of water into a drizzle.
  5. Build. Bowl the quinoa, greens, veg, and chicken; drizzle with sauce.
Lean tip
Thin the tahini with extra lemon and water to keep the drizzle light, or swap for fat-free yogurt.

title: Tofu & Edamame Stir-Fry
summary: Crisp tofu and edamame in a quick ginger-garlic sauce. A plant-based, high-protein stir-fry that stays lean with tamari and minimal oil.
body:
Why this works

Pressing and dry-searing extra-firm tofu gives a crisp edge without deep-frying. Edamame adds a second complete protein and a pop of color.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 1 block extra-firm tofu (~350g), pressed & cubed
  • 1 cup shelled edamame · 2 cups mixed stir-fry veg
  • 2 tbsp tamari · 1 tbsp rice vinegar · 1 tsp sesame oil
  • 1 tbsp grated ginger · 2 garlic cloves · 1 tsp cornstarch

Method

  1. Crisp tofu. Sear cubed tofu in a hot nonstick pan until golden on most sides; remove.
  2. Stir-fry veg. Add veg and edamame; toss over high heat 3–4 min until crisp-tender.
  3. Sauce. Add ginger and garlic 30 sec, then tamari, vinegar, sesame oil, and cornstarch slurry.
  4. Combine. Return tofu; toss until glossy and coated. Serve.
Lean tip
Use tamari for gluten-free and skip extra oil — the nonstick pan crisps tofu with very little.

title: Sheet-Pan Lemon Chicken & Asparagus
summary: Everything roasts on one tray: lean chicken and crisp asparagus with lemon and garlic. Minimal cleanup, maximum protein.
body:
Why this works

Chicken thighs (or breast) need more time than asparagus, so they get a head start; the spears go in for just the last stretch and stay snappy.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 4 boneless skinless chicken thighs (or 2 breasts)
  • 1 bunch asparagus, trimmed
  • 1 tbsp olive oil · 3 garlic cloves · 1 lemon
  • Salt, pepper, paprika

Method

  1. Preheat. Heat the oven to 220°C.
  2. Season & roast chicken. Toss chicken with oil, garlic, paprika, salt; roast 15 min.
  3. Add asparagus. Add the spears and lemon slices to the tray; roast 8–10 min more.
  4. Check. Chicken should read 74°C and asparagus be tender-crisp.
  5. Finish. Squeeze the roasted lemon over everything and serve.
Lean tip
Use chicken breast and halve the oil for a ~280-cal plate with the same protein.

title: Steamed Ginger-Scallion White Fish
summary: Silky steamed white fish finished with sizzling ginger, scallion, and a splash of tamari. Restaurant-classic, barely any fat.
body:
Why this works

Gentle steam keeps lean fish from drying out, and the final hot-oil pour blooms the aromatics in seconds for a glossy, savory finish.

Ingredients (serves 2)

  • 2 white fish fillets (cod, sole, or sea bass; ~170g each)
  • Thumb of ginger, julienned · 3 scallions, sliced
  • 2 tbsp tamari · 1 tsp sugar · 1 tbsp neutral oil
  • Cilantro · pinch white pepper

Method

  1. Set up the steamer. Bring 2cm water to a simmer with a rack or heatproof plate.
  2. Steam. Lay fish on a plate with half the ginger; steam covered 7–9 min until it flakes.
  3. Sauce. Warm tamari with sugar and a splash of the steaming water; pour over the fish.
  4. Sizzle. Top with scallion and remaining ginger; pour over the smoking-hot oil.
  5. Serve. Finish with cilantro and white pepper.
Lean tip
Use just 1 tsp of oil for the sizzle — you only need enough to bloom the aromatics.

title: Dried Black Beans, No Soak
summary: A pound of dried black beans goes from bag to creamy in one pot with no overnight soak. Thirty minutes at pressure, twenty minutes of natural release, and you have five days of beans in their own broth.
body:
Why this works

Dried beans do not need an overnight soak in a pressure cooker. At high pressure the water sits around 120°C instead of 100°C, so a hard bean hydrates and softens in the same half hour it would take just to come to a simmer on the stove. Skipping the soak actually gives you better beans — more of the flavor stays in the pot instead of going down the drain.

The part people get wrong is the release. Beans foam. A quick release pulls that starchy foam up through the valve, splits the skins, and leaves you scrubbing the lid. Let the pot come down on its own and the beans stay whole.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 450g (1 lb) dried black beans, sorted and rinsed
  • 1.4L (6 cups) water — a 1:3 ratio by weight
  • 1 tbsp olive oil · 1 onion, diced
  • 4 garlic cloves, smashed · 2 tsp ground cumin
  • 1 bay leaf · ½ tsp dried oregano
  • 2 tsp kosher salt · juice of ½ lime

Method

  1. Sort and rinse. Spread the beans on a sheet pan and pull out any stones, clumps of dirt, or shriveled beans. Rinse in a colander until the water runs clear.
  2. Build a base. Set the pot to Sauté on normal. Cook the onion in the oil 4–5 min until soft and translucent, then add the garlic, cumin, and oregano and stir 30 sec until fragrant. Press Cancel.
  3. Load the pot. Add the beans, water, bay leaf, and salt. Stir once and scrape the bottom clean so no stuck onion triggers a burn warning. The liquid must sit below the two-thirds max line — beans expand.
  4. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve set to Sealing. A full pot of cold water takes about 12 min to pressurize. That is not part of the cook time and the display does not start counting until it gets there.
  5. Pressure cook 30 min. High pressure, 30 min for beans that are creamy but hold their shape. Push to 35 min if you want them soft enough to mash for refried beans.
  6. Natural release 20 min. Leave the valve alone for a full 20 min. Never quick release beans straight off the cook — the foam clogs the float valve and blows the skins off. Vent whatever pressure is left after that.
  7. Season and rest. Pull the bay leaf, stir in the lime, taste for salt. Let them sit 5 min in their liquid; they firm up slightly and the broth thickens as it cools.
If they came out hard
Old beans are almost always the cause, not the pot — beans over a year old can take twice as long. Lock the lid back on and run another 8–10 min at high pressure with a natural release. There is no penalty for a second round.

Storage

Store the beans in their cooking liquid. It keeps them from drying out at the edges and it is a genuinely good broth for soup. Fridge 5 days, freezer 3 months. Freeze in 1½-cup portions with a little liquid — that is about one drained can.

title: Chickpeas from Dry (and Hummus)
summary: A pound of dry chickpeas cooked soft enough that the skins fall apart on their own, then half of it blended into hummus. No soak, no peeling, and you keep the cooking liquid.
body:
Why this works

Chickpeas are the densest common legume and they are stubborn — unsoaked, they need 45 min at high pressure, roughly twice what a black bean wants. A teaspoon of baking soda raises the pH of the water, which breaks down pectin in the cell walls and dissolves the skins. That is the entire secret to hummus that is silky instead of grainy, and it means you never have to sit there peeling chickpeas one at a time.

The trade-off: soda makes them soft. If you want firm chickpeas to roast or throw in a salad, leave it out and cut the cook to 35 min.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 450g (1 lb) dried chickpeas, sorted and rinsed
  • 1.9L (8 cups) water — a 1:4 ratio, they drink a lot
  • 1 tsp baking soda · 1 tsp kosher salt
  • For hummus: 3 cups cooked chickpeas, drained
  • 90g tahini · juice of 1½ lemons · 1 garlic clove
  • ½ tsp cumin · ½ tsp salt · 1 ice cube
  • 60–120ml reserved cooking liquid

Method

  1. Sort and rinse. Check for stones, rinse in a colander until the water runs clear, and drain.
  2. Load the pot. Chickpeas, 8 cups water, baking soda, salt. Stir once. Soda plus chickpeas foams hard, so keep the total volume at or below the half line even though the pot allows two-thirds for most things.
  3. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve sealed. Eight cups of cold water takes about 13 min to pressurize. The cook timer does not start until then.
  4. Pressure cook 45 min. High pressure, 45 min for hummus-soft chickpeas that squash between two fingers with no resistance. Use 35 min if you want them intact for salads and roasting.
  5. Natural release 20 min. No quick release, ever, on this one. Soda-foamed chickpea water goes straight out the valve and across your cabinets. Vent the remainder after 20 min.
  6. Drain and reserve. Drain over a bowl and keep at least 2 cups of the cooking liquid — that is aquafaba, and it is what makes the hummus loose without adding oil. Skim off any loose skins floating on top.
  7. Blend the hummus. Whip the tahini, lemon juice, garlic, cumin, and salt alone for 60 sec until it seizes and turns pale. Add 3 cups of still-warm chickpeas and run 2 min, then stream in cooking liquid and drop in the ice cube. Blend a full 3–4 min more — it should climb the sides and look glossy.
Why the ice cube
Long blending heats tahini and turns it dull and slightly bitter. One ice cube keeps the temperature down and whips air in, which is what makes restaurant hummus look fluffy instead of pasty.

Storage

Keep leftover chickpeas submerged in their liquid: fridge 5 days, freezer 3 months. Hummus keeps 5 days with a thin film of olive oil poured over the surface to stop it drying out. Freeze extra aquafaba in an ice cube tray — two cubes thin out hummus later, and it whips like egg white.

title: Perfect White Rice, Hands Off
summary: Long-grain white rice at a 1:1 water ratio, four minutes at pressure, ten minutes of rest. Separate grains every time with nothing to watch and no pot to babysit.
body:
Why this works

Stovetop rice recipes call for 1½ to 2 parts water because a good chunk of it boils off. A sealed pressure cooker loses nothing, so the only water you need is the water the grain actually absorbs — that is 1:1 by volume for long-grain white rice, and going higher is exactly why rice comes out wet.

Four minutes of high pressure sounds impossibly short, and it is, on its own. The grain also cooks through the 7-minute ramp up to pressure and through the 10-minute natural release, when the pot is still well above boiling. Those three phases together are the recipe; treat any one of them as optional and you get crunchy centers or mush.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 2 cups (about 370g) long-grain white rice — jasmine or basmati
  • 2 cups (475ml) water
  • 1 tsp kosher salt
  • 1 tsp neutral oil or butter (optional, keeps grains separate)

Method

  1. Rinse until it runs clear. Swirl the rice in a bowl of cold water and pour it off, three or four changes, until the water is no longer cloudy. This strips loose surface starch, which is what makes rice clump and what makes the pot foam.
  2. Drain hard. Shake the strainer properly. Water clinging to wet rice counts toward your 2 cups, and a quarter cup of it is the difference between fluffy and sticky.
  3. Load and level. Rice, water, salt, and the oil if using. Stir once, then shake the pot flat so every grain is submerged. Uneven rice cooks unevenly.
  4. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve sealed. This much cold water pressurizes in about 7 min. The 4-minute display does not begin until the float valve pops.
  5. Pressure cook 4 min. High pressure. Use 3 min for basmati, 4 for jasmine, 5 for a shorter or stickier grain.
  6. Natural release 10 min. Set a timer and walk away. Quick releasing rice right off the cook drops the pressure so fast that water flashes to steam inside the grains and tears them open — that is the gummy, blown-out rice everyone blames on the machine.
  7. Vent, fluff, and rest. Release any remaining pressure, then fork the rice from the outside edge toward the middle in a lifting motion. Leave the lid off 3 min so the surface steam escapes.
Scaling up
The ratio stays 1:1 and the cook time stays 4 min from 1 cup all the way to 4 cups — only the come-to-pressure ramp gets longer, roughly 5 min for a single cup and 10 for four. Never fill past the half line; rice foams.

Storage

Spread leftovers on a plate to cool fast, then refrigerate within an hour — cooked rice left warm on the counter is one of the few genuine food-safety risks in a home kitchen. Fridge 4 days. It freezes better than it keeps: press it flat in a bag, then reheat from frozen with a tablespoon of water, covered, 90 sec in the microwave.

title: Brown Rice That Isn't Mush
summary: Brown rice at 1:1.25 water, 22 minutes at pressure, then a rest with the lid off. The bran stays intact and the grains stay separate instead of collapsing into paste.
body:
Why this works

Brown rice is white rice with the bran and germ still on. That bran layer is a waterproof jacket — it resists absorption, which is why brown rice takes 45 min in a covered pot on the stove and still comes out chalky in the middle sometimes. Pressure forces water through it in 22 min.

Mushy brown rice is almost never a timing problem. It is a water problem: people carry over the 2:1 ratio from the stovetop, where a third of the water evaporates, into a sealed pot where none does. Use 1.25 parts water to 1 part rice and the grain absorbs essentially all of it. Then rest it uncovered — that last step is doing more work than you think.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 2 cups (about 370g) long-grain brown rice
  • 2½ cups (590ml) water
  • 1 tsp kosher salt
  • 1 tsp neutral oil (optional, cuts foaming)

Method

  1. Rinse and drain well. Two changes of cold water is enough — brown rice sheds far less surface starch than white. Drain it thoroughly; clinging water throws the ratio off.
  2. Load and level. Rice, water, salt, oil. Stir once and shake the pot flat so the rice sits in an even bed under the water.
  3. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve sealed. Roughly 8 min for this volume. The cook time on the display starts only after that.
  4. Pressure cook 22 min. High pressure. Brown basmati wants 20 min, short-grain brown 24. Note it is 22 min for a full pot or a half pot — volume changes the ramp, not the cook.
  5. Natural release 10 min. Bran foams even harder than white rice starch. Ten minutes untouched, then vent whatever is left through the valve.
  6. Fluff. Fork it up from the edges toward the center, lifting rather than stirring, so you do not mash the grains against the pot.
  7. Rest uncovered 3 min. This is the single biggest difference between separate grains and a sticky block. Surface moisture steams off and the grains firm up. Do not leave it sealed on Keep Warm.
Diagnose the result
Wet and pasty means too much water — drop to 1:1.2 next time. Chalky or hard in the center means not enough time — add 2 min, do not add water. Old rice from the back of the cupboard usually wants the extra 2 min.

Storage

Cool it spread out, then refrigerate within an hour. Fridge 4 days, freezer 3 months. Brown rice reheats better than white because the bran holds structure: a splash of water and 90 sec covered in the microwave brings it right back. It is the best base in this catalog for meal-prep bowls — it does not go gluey after a few days like white rice can.

title: Batch Steel-Cut Oats
summary: Six breakfasts in one pot: toast the oats in fat, four minutes at pressure, fifteen minutes of natural release. No stirring, no pot boiling over on the stove.
body:
Why this works

Steel-cut oats are whole oat groats chopped into pieces, not rolled flat, so water has to work its way into a dense chunk of grain. On the stove that is 30 min of stirring and a pot that boils over the moment you look away. At pressure it is 4 min of cook time and nothing to watch.

Two things make the difference. Toasting the oats in fat first, which takes three minutes and turns them genuinely nutty instead of flat. And a 1:3 ratio — less than that and you get gluey oats that scorch on the bottom.

Oats foam violently. This is the one recipe where a quick release will actually spray hot starch out of the valve, so the 15-minute natural release is not a suggestion.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 2 cups (about 340g) steel-cut oats
  • 6 cups (1.4L) water — a 1:3 ratio
  • 1 tbsp coconut oil or butter
  • ¾ tsp kosher salt · 1 tsp cinnamon (optional)
  • To finish: milk, maple syrup, or fruit, per bowl

Method

  1. Toast the oats. Set the pot to Sauté on normal, melt the oil, then add the dry oats and stir 3–4 min. They will darken about a shade and smell like toast. Press Cancel.
  2. Add liquid and salt. Pour in the water and scrape the bottom clean with a wooden spoon — toasted oat stuck to the base is the classic cause of a burn warning. Add salt and cinnamon. Stay at or below the half line; oats expand and foam.
  3. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve sealed. Eight cups of volume takes about 10 min to pressurize.
  4. Pressure cook 4 min. High pressure. Drop to 3 min for oats with real chew, go to 6 min for soft porridge.
  5. Natural release 15 min. Do not touch the valve. Oat foam under pressure sprays a fine mist of starch across the ceiling if you vent early, and it clogs the anti-block shield. Release whatever is left after 15 min.
  6. Stir hard. The surface will look watery and separated when you open it. Stir for 30 sec and it pulls together into porridge as it cools — do not add thickener, and do not run it longer next time.
  7. Portion. Divide into six containers while still hot. Leave the toppings off until you eat them.
Milk goes in after
Dairy scorches on the bottom of the pot under pressure and reliably trips the burn sensor. Cook in plain water, then stir milk or cream into the individual bowl. Same for maple syrup — sugar burns on the base too.

Storage

Fridge 5 days. They set very firm when cold, which is normal — add 2 tbsp of water or milk and microwave 60–90 sec, stirring halfway. For longer storage, portion into a muffin tin, freeze solid, and bag the pucks: one puck plus a splash of milk is a 2-minute breakfast for three months.

title: Pulled Pork Shoulder
summary: Four pounds of pork shoulder cut into chunks and cooked 55 minutes at high pressure, then shredded and dressed with its own reduced juices. Plan on about two and a quarter hours door to door.
body:
Why this works

Pork shoulder is collagen, and collagen only turns to gelatin after a long stretch above 70°C. Cutting the roast into four fist-sized chunks roughly triples the exposed surface, so 55 minutes at high pressure does what six hours in a low oven does. The pot adds no browning of its own, which is why the sear on Sauté is not optional — skip it and you get pale, boiled-tasting meat.

Ingredients (serves 8)

  • 1.8 kg (4 lb) boneless pork shoulder, cut into 4 chunks
  • 1 tbsp kosher salt · 2 tsp black pepper · 2 tsp smoked paprika
  • 1 tbsp brown sugar · 1 tsp garlic powder · 1 tsp onion powder
  • 1 tbsp neutral oil · 1 large onion, sliced
  • 240ml (1 cup) chicken broth · 2 tbsp cider vinegar · 1 tbsp tomato paste

Method

  1. Trim and rub. Cut the shoulder into 4 chunks, leaving a thin fat cap on each. Mix the salt, pepper, paprika, sugar, garlic powder and onion powder and rub it over every face.
  2. Sear in batches. Sauté on High until the oil shimmers, then brown two chunks at a time, 3–4 min a side. Four chunks at once drops the pot temperature and they steam instead. Move each batch to a plate.
  3. Deglaze. Cook the onion 2 min, pour in the broth and vinegar, and scrape every brown spot off the base with a wooden spoon. Anything still stuck there will read as a burn notice later. Stir in the tomato paste, then turn Sauté off.
  4. Cook under pressure. Return the pork and its plate juices. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure 55 min. Budget another 15 min before that: a full pot takes that long to come up to pressure, and the display shows nothing but "On" while it does.
  5. Natural release. When it beeps, walk away for 20 min. Venting early drops the pressure faster than the meat can re-absorb its juices, and the fibers seize. Then flip the valve for whatever is left.
  6. Shred. Lift the pork out with tongs and pull it apart with two forks, discarding the thick fat seams as you find them.
  7. Reduce and dress. Sauté High and boil the liquid down by about half, 8–10 min. Skim the fat off the top, then pour 1–1½ cups back over the pork until it is glossy and wet.
Avoiding the burn notice
Keep at least 1 cup of thin liquid in the pot and add the tomato paste last, stirred through — sugary purees sink to the base and scorch against the element.

Storage

Refrigerates 4 days, but store it submerged in its own liquid or it dries out overnight. Freezes 3 months in 2-cup portions; reheat covered with a splash of the juices rather than dry in a pan.

title: Chuck Pot Roast with Potatoes and Carrots
summary: Chuck cut into three pieces goes 45 minutes at high pressure, then the potatoes and carrots get a separate 5-minute run so they arrive tender instead of dissolved. One pot, gravy included.
body:
Why this works

Chuck is hard-worked shoulder muscle laced with connective tissue, and it goes through a tough phase before it goes tender. Left whole, a 1.4 kg roast needs about 70 minutes; cut into three thick pieces it is shreddable in 45. The vegetables cannot survive that, so they get their own short cycle afterwards — five minutes at pressure on already-hot liquid.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 1.4 kg (3 lb) boneless chuck roast, cut into 3 pieces
  • 2 tsp kosher salt · 1 tsp black pepper · 1 tbsp neutral oil
  • 1 large onion, sliced · 4 garlic cloves, smashed
  • 480ml (2 cups) beef broth · 2 tbsp tomato paste · 1 tbsp tamari
  • 2 sprigs thyme · 1 bay leaf
  • 700g baby potatoes, halved · 4 carrots, cut into 5cm pieces
  • 2 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 2 tbsp cold water

Method

  1. Season and sear. Salt and pepper all three pieces. Sauté High, oil in, then sear one or two pieces at a time about 4 min a side until properly dark. This is the only browning the dish gets.
  2. Onion and deglaze. Set the beef aside. Soften the onion and garlic 3 min, then pour in the broth and tamari and scrape the base clean. Stir in the tomato paste and the herbs, and turn Sauté off.
  3. Pressure cook the beef. Return the beef, lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure 45 min. Reckon on about 13 min for the pot to come to pressure first — that is on top of the 45.
  4. Natural release 15 min. Let the pressure fall on its own. This is where the meat re-absorbs liquid; cutting it short gives you tough beef in a thin sauce. Vent the remainder.
  5. Add the vegetables. Tuck the potatoes and carrots around the beef, sitting them in the liquid. Do not fill past the 2⁄3 line.
  6. Second short cycle. Lid on, High Pressure 5 min. Coming back to pressure on hot liquid takes about 8 min. Quick release the moment it beeps — every extra minute is more mush.
  7. Gravy. Lift out the beef and vegetables. Skim the fat, fish out the bay and thyme stems, then Sauté High and whisk in the cornstarch slurry. It thickens in 2–3 min. Shred or slice the beef and spoon the gravy over.
Why two stages
Potatoes and carrots need 4–5 min at pressure. Anything held at 45 min collapses into the sauce. If you only want one cycle, cut the vegetables into large 8cm chunks and accept that they will be very soft.

Storage

Keeps 4 days refrigerated with the gravy poured over the meat. The potatoes go grainy in the freezer, so freeze the beef and gravy alone, up to 3 months. Reheat gently — a hard boil dries the chuck out again.

title: Whole Chicken in 25 Minutes
summary: A 4 lb bird on a trivet, 6 minutes per pound at high pressure, then five minutes under the broiler for skin worth eating. The 25 minutes is cook time only; the whole job runs about 95.
body:
Why this works

The working rule is 6 minutes per pound at high pressure, so a 1.8 kg (4 lb) bird gets 25 minutes. That number is the cook cycle alone — a full pot needs roughly 12 minutes to come up to pressure and 15 more to release naturally, which is where the honest hour goes. A 6-quart pot fits a 4–5 lb chicken and no more; anything larger will not clear the rim with the lid on.

Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 1 whole chicken, 1.8–2.2 kg (4–5 lb), giblets removed
  • 2 tsp kosher salt · 1 tsp black pepper · 1 tsp smoked paprika
  • 1 tsp garlic powder · ½ tsp dried thyme
  • 1 tbsp neutral oil · ½ lemon · 3 garlic cloves
  • 240ml (1 cup) chicken broth · the trivet that came with the pot

Method

  1. Dry and season. Pat the bird bone-dry inside and out — wet skin will not brown. Mix the salt and spices and rub them over the skin and into the cavity. Put the lemon half and garlic cloves inside and tie the legs together.
  2. Sear breast-side down. Sauté High with the oil, then lower the chicken in breast-first and leave it 5–6 min without moving it. Flip it, give the back 2 min, and lift it out onto a plate.
  3. Deglaze and set the trivet. Pour in the broth and scrape the base clean, then drop the trivet in and set the chicken on it breast-side up. The trivet keeps the bird out of the liquid so it steams rather than poaches.
  4. Cook under pressure. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure 25 min for 4 lb, 30 min for 5 lb. Expect about 12 min of silence first while it pressurizes.
  5. Natural release 15 min. Do not vent early. A quick release on a whole bird squeezes juice straight out of the breast. Release any remainder after 15 min.
  6. Check and lift out. The thickest part of the thigh should read 74°C. If it is short, lid back on and 5 more minutes at pressure. Lift the chicken onto a foil-lined tray.
  7. Broil the skin. Under a hot broiler 5–7 min until the skin is brown and taut. Watch it — the sugar in the paprika catches fast.
  8. Rest and carve. Rest 10 min before carving. Strain the pot liquid and use it as a light jus or as stock.
Skin
Pressure-cooked skin comes out slack and grey. The broiler step is what makes this a roast chicken instead of a poached one, and it takes five minutes.

Storage

Carve the meat off the frame the same day and refrigerate up to 4 days. The carcass plus the strained pot liquid makes stock — 45 min at high pressure, no trivet.

title: Shredded Chicken, Fresh or Frozen
summary: Two pounds of boneless breast into six servings of shreds for bowls, tacos, and salads. Fresh takes 10 minutes at pressure, straight-from-frozen takes 15 with no thawing.
body:
Why this works

Pressure steam gets into frozen meat as fast as it gets into fresh, so there is no thawing step — frozen breasts just need about half again as long. Fresh: 10 min at high pressure. Frozen: 15 min. Add roughly 10 min for the pot to come to pressure and 10 min of natural release either way, which is the real reason this is an hour and not twenty minutes.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 900g (2 lb) boneless skinless chicken breasts, fresh or frozen solid
  • 1 tbsp neutral oil · 2 tsp kosher salt · 1 tsp black pepper
  • 1 tsp cumin · 1 tsp smoked paprika · 1 tsp garlic powder
  • 240ml (1 cup) chicken broth · juice of ½ lime

Method

  1. Bloom the spices. Sauté on Normal with the oil, then the cumin, paprika and garlic powder for 45 seconds until they smell toasted. Dry spices in hot oil taste twice as strong as spices stirred into broth.
  2. Deglaze. Pour in the broth immediately and scrape the base clean before the spices catch. A film of scorched spice on the base is the most common burn notice in this recipe.
  3. Lay the chicken in. Salt and pepper the breasts and set them in a single layer in the liquid. If they are frozen, separate them — a stuck-together block cooks unevenly and the middle stays raw.
  4. Cook under pressure. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure: 10 min for fresh, 15 min for frozen. Add 5 min for thighs. The pot takes about 10 min to pressurize before the count starts.
  5. Natural release 10 min. This matters more with lean breast than with anything else — a fast release makes it stringy and dry. Quick release whatever is left after 10 min.
  6. Check and shred. The thickest breast should read 74°C. Shred with two forks, or drop the whole lot into a stand mixer with the paddle on low for 20 seconds.
  7. Moisten. Sauté the remaining liquid down to about 1 cup, 4–5 min, then stir it back through the shreds with the lime juice. Dry shredded chicken is chicken that was drained.
Frozen, honestly
Straight from the freezer works, but only if the breasts go in as separate pieces. Freeze them flat and individually wrapped and you never have to plan ahead.

Storage

Four days refrigerated in its liquid, or freeze in 1-cup portions with a few spoonfuls of the cooking liquid for 3 months. It thaws in a bowl of water in about 20 min.

title: Baby Back Ribs, Fall-Off-the-Bone
summary: One rack cut in half, stood on edge around the trivet, 25 minutes at high pressure and a long natural release. Five minutes under the broiler sets the glaze.
body:
Why this works

Twenty-five minutes at high pressure takes baby backs past tender and into fall-off-the-bone; 20 minutes leaves a little chew if you prefer that. Ribs are the one cut here you do not sear — there is no room, and the broiler at the end does the same job better. Stand the rack on edge in a coil around the trivet and a 6-quart pot swallows a full rack with room for the steam to circulate.

Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 1 rack baby back ribs, about 1.1 kg (2½ lb)
  • 1 tbsp brown sugar · 2 tsp kosher salt · 1 tsp black pepper
  • 2 tsp smoked paprika · 1 tsp garlic powder · ½ tsp cayenne
  • 240ml (1 cup) water · 2 tbsp cider vinegar · 1 tsp liquid smoke (optional)
  • 240ml (1 cup) barbecue sauce (check the label if you need it gluten-free)

Method

  1. Pull the membrane. Slide a butter knife under the silverskin on the bone side, get a grip with a paper towel, and peel it off in one sheet. Leave it on and the rub never reaches the meat and the ribs eat rubbery.
  2. Rub and rest. Mix the sugar, salt, pepper, paprika, garlic powder and cayenne and press it into both faces. Cut the rack in half so it fits. Ten minutes on the counter is enough for the salt to start working.
  3. Load the pot. Water, vinegar and liquid smoke into the base, then the trivet, then stand the rib halves on edge curled around the inside wall, meat side out. Keep the liquid under the trivet, not on the ribs.
  4. Cook under pressure. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure 25 min. Add about 12 min for the pot to reach pressure first. Use 20 min if you want them to hold together on the bone.
  5. Natural release 15 min. Full natural release is what keeps the meat from tightening back onto the bone. Vent the remainder after 15 min and lift the racks out carefully — they are barely holding together.
  6. Sauce. Move the ribs to a foil-lined tray, meat side up, and brush a thick coat of barbecue sauce over the top. Preheat the broiler while the pot releases.
  7. Broil. 5–7 min about 15cm from the element, until the sauce bubbles and darkens at the edges. It goes from glazed to burnt in under a minute, so stay at the oven.
  8. Rest and cut. Rest 5 min, then cut between the bones with the rack meat side down so you can see where they are.
Burn notice
Barbecue sauce never goes in the pot. Sugar on the base scorches within a minute of the element coming on — the only liquid under the trivet should be water and vinegar.

Storage

Refrigerate cut ribs 3 days, wrapped tight in foil. Reheat wrapped at 160°C for 15 min rather than in the microwave, which drives the fat out. They freeze 2 months, sauced.

title: Beef and Bean Chili
summary: Ground beef, beans, and a thick tomato base that tastes like it simmered all afternoon. Fifteen minutes at pressure, plus the come-up and release.
body:
Why this works

Pressure gives you the melded, long-simmered flavor of a three-hour pot in 15 minutes of cook time. The catch is the burn notice. A thick tomato base is dense and sugary, and it scorches on the bottom of the inner pot before the machine ever reaches pressure — then the sensor cuts the heat and you get a raw pot of chili and an error code. You beat it two ways: deglaze until the bottom is genuinely clean, and pour the crushed tomatoes on top at the end without stirring them in. The thin broth underneath is what circulates and lifts the lid to pressure.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 900g ground beef, 80/20 or coarse-ground chuck
  • 1 large onion, diced · 1 red pepper, diced · 4 garlic cloves, minced
  • 3 tbsp chili powder · 1 tbsp cumin · 2 tsp smoked paprika · 1 tsp dried oregano
  • 2 tbsp tomato paste · 1½ tsp kosher salt · black pepper
  • 1½ cups (360ml) beef broth
  • 2 cans (400g each) kidney or pinto beans, rinsed
  • 1 can (800g) crushed tomatoes — goes on top, unstirred

Method

  1. Brown the beef. Sauté on High. Break the beef into the dry pot and let it sit before you stir it — you want brown crust, not gray steam. About 8 min. Spoon off all but a tablespoon of fat.
  2. Soften the aromatics. Add onion and pepper, cook 4 min. Add garlic, spices, and tomato paste and stir 1 min until the spices smell toasted and the paste darkens.
  3. Deglaze until the bottom is clean. Pour in the broth and scrape every stuck patch loose with a wooden spoon. Run the spoon across the whole base — if it catches, keep scraping. Press Cancel.
  4. Layer, do not stir. Scatter the rinsed beans over the meat, then pour the crushed tomatoes on top and level them. Leave them sitting there. Stirring now is what earns you the burn notice.
  5. Pressure cook 15 min. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure, 15 min. Expect about 12 min to come up to pressure before the timer even starts.
  6. Release. Natural release 10 min, then flip the valve for the rest. Venting a full pot cold sprays chili through the valve and all over the cupboard.
  7. Stir and thicken. Now stir it into one thing. If it is looser than you want, simmer on Sauté 5 min uncovered, stirring. Taste for salt, then add a splash of vinegar or lime to wake it up.
If you get a burn notice anyway
Cancel, release pressure, and lift the insert out. Scrape the bottom clean into a bowl, leave the scorched crust behind, add ¼ cup water, and restart. Nothing is ruined unless you keep cooking on top of it.

Storage

Better on day two. Fridge 4 days in an airtight container, freezer 3 months. Cool it in a shallow pan first so it drops below 5°C fast, then portion. Reheat with a splash of broth — it tightens up cold.

title: Red Lentil Dal
summary: Red lentils cooked to a smooth puree in five minutes at pressure, finished with a hot tadka of cumin and chili. Cheap, fast, and genuinely filling.
body:
Why this works

Red lentils have no skin, so they collapse into a puree on their own — there is nothing to stir and nothing to watch. Five minutes at pressure takes them all the way down. The part people get wrong is the release. Split lentils throw off starchy foam, and cracking the valve early sends that froth up through the vent, where it clogs the float. Let the pressure fall on its own for a full 15 minutes. The tadka goes on at the very end so the whole spices stay sharp instead of stewing into the pot.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 1½ cups (300g) red lentils (masoor dal), rinsed until the water runs clear
  • 4 cups (1L) water
  • 1 onion, diced · 4 garlic cloves, minced · 1 tbsp grated ginger
  • 2 tomatoes, chopped, or 1 cup canned
  • 1 tsp turmeric · 1 tsp ground coriander · 2 tsp kosher salt
  • Tadka: 3 tbsp neutral oil or ghee · 1 tsp cumin seeds · 2 dried red chilies · ¼ tsp asafoetida · 1 tsp Kashmiri chili powder
  • Juice of ½ lemon · handful of cilantro

Method

  1. Rinse the lentils properly. Swirl them in a bowl of cold water and pour it off, three or four changes, until the water runs clear. That loose surface starch is exactly what makes the pot foam later.
  2. Sauté the aromatics. Sauté on Normal with 1 tbsp oil. Onion 4 min until translucent, then ginger and garlic 1 min, then turmeric and coriander 30 sec — no longer, ground spices burn.
  3. Tomatoes, and deglaze. Add the tomatoes with a splash of water and scrape the base clean while they break down, about 2 min. Press Cancel.
  4. Load and pressure cook 5 min. Add lentils, 4 cups water, and salt. Stir once so nothing sits dry on the bottom. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure, 5 min. It takes about 10 min to come up first.
  5. Full natural release. Do not touch the valve for 15 min. Wait for the float valve to drop by itself. This is not optional with dal.
  6. Make the tadka. While it depressurizes, heat the remaining 2 tbsp oil in a small pan until it shimmers. Cumin seeds until they pop and darken, about 30 sec, then the chilies and asafoetida for 10 sec, then pull it off the heat and stir in the chili powder.
  7. Finish. Whisk the dal smooth — it thickens as it sits, so thin it with hot water to a pourable consistency. Pour the tadka over the top, add lemon and cilantro, and taste for salt.
Never quick release this
Foaming pots — dal, split peas, oatmeal, pasta — spit through the valve under a hard release. If you are in a hurry, wait the 15 min anyway and use the time to cook rice.

Storage

Fridge 5 days, freezer 3 months. It sets almost solid when cold; reheat with a good splash of water and whisk it back together. Make the tadka fresh for reheated portions — it is 90 seconds and most of the flavor.

title: Chicken Stock in 45 Minutes
summary: Clear, gelatinous chicken stock from bones and scraps. The 45 minutes is time at pressure, not door to door - budget about two hours all in.

nutrition.serving: Per 1 cup (makes about 2.5 L, roughly 10 cups)

body:
Why this works

A sealed pot holds the liquid above boiling without ever letting it move. You get the collagen extraction of a six-hour simmer with none of the churning that emulsifies fat and scum into the liquid, which is why pressure stock comes out clear and sets to a firm jelly in the fridge. Be honest with yourself about the clock, though: 45 minutes is time at pressure. Add roughly 15 minutes to come up, 20 to come down, and 15 to brown and strain.

Ingredients (makes about 2.5 L)

  • 1.5–2 kg chicken bones: backs, wings, feet, or a picked-over roast carcass
  • 1 tbsp neutral oil
  • 2 onions, quartered, skins left on for color
  • 2 carrots and 3 celery ribs, in big chunks
  • 1 head of garlic, halved crosswise
  • 10 black peppercorns · 2 bay leaves · a handful of parsley stems
  • Cold water to the 2/3 max line, roughly 2.5 L

Method

  1. Brown the bones. Sauté on High with the oil. Work in two batches, 4 min each, until the bones take real color. Skip this and you get a pale, thin-tasting stock.
  2. Deglaze. Splash in a cup of water and scrape the base completely clean. Everything you just built is stuck to the bottom; it belongs in the stock, not welded to the pot. Press Cancel.
  3. Fill to 2/3 and no further. Return all the bones, add the vegetables and aromatics, then cold water up to the 2/3 line stamped inside the pot. Never past it. Stock foams under pressure and a fuller pot pushes froth into the valve.
  4. Pressure cook 45 min. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure, 45 min. A pot this full and this cold takes about 15 min to reach pressure.
  5. Natural release, all the way. 20 min minimum, until the float drops on its own. Venting hot fatty liquid sprays grease and churns the pot cloudy right at the finish line.
  6. Strain, do not press. Ladle through a fine sieve lined with a damp cloth into a bowl. Let it drip. Pressing the solids forces fine particles through and turns clear stock murky.
  7. Cool it fast. Divide into shallow containers or set the bowl in an ice bath. Get it under 5°C within two hours, then chill overnight and lift the solid fat cap off the top.
The 2/3 line is not a suggestion
It is printed inside the pot for foaming foods, and stock is the classic one. Overfill and froth reaches the vent, the float valve sticks, and the machine stops regulating properly. Fewer bones, not more water, if you need room.

Storage

Fridge 5 days, freezer 6 months. Freeze in 1-cup portions or in an ice cube tray for splashes. Do not salt the stock — season the dish you use it in, so a reduction does not turn brutal. Good stock will be solid jelly cold; that gelatin is the point.

title: Chicken Soup from Scratch
summary: Bone-in thighs build the broth and give you the meat, all in one pot. Noodles go in at the end on Saute, never under pressure.
body:
Why this works

Bone-in thighs do two jobs at once. Twelve minutes at pressure pulls collagen out of the bones and gives you body you would otherwise need a separate stock for, while the dark meat stays moist enough to shred instead of drying out the way breast does. Noodles never go under pressure — they come out as paste, and their starch is exactly the kind of thing that foams through the valve. They cook at the end in the residual heat on Sauté, which takes about as long as it takes you to shred the chicken.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 1kg bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs (about 6–8)
  • 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 1 onion, 3 carrots, and 3 celery ribs, all diced
  • 4 garlic cloves, minced
  • 8 cups (2L) chicken stock or water
  • 2 bay leaves · 1 tsp dried thyme · 2 tsp kosher salt · black pepper
  • 150g wide egg noodles
  • Juice of ½ lemon · a big handful of dill, chopped

Method

  1. Brown the thighs skin down. Sauté on High with the oil. Lay the thighs skin-side down and leave them 6 min — they release when they are ready. Remove to a plate. Pull the skin off now if you want a leaner soup; the rendered fat has already done its work.
  2. Sweat the mirepoix. Onion, carrot, and celery into the fat for 5 min until the onion is soft, then garlic and thyme for 30 sec.
  3. Deglaze. Pour in a cup of the stock and scrape the browned bits off the base until the spoon glides. A clean bottom is the whole difference between soup and a burn notice. Press Cancel.
  4. Pressure cook 12 min. Return the thighs with any juices, add the rest of the stock, bay leaves, salt, and pepper. Lid on, valve sealed, High Pressure, 12 min. Two liters of cold liquid takes about 12 min to reach pressure.
  5. Release gently. Natural release 10 min, then vent the rest. A pot this full sputters broth if you crack it hot.
  6. Shred. Lift the thighs out with tongs, shred with two forks, and discard the bones, skin, and bay leaves. Skim any fat pooling on the surface.
  7. Noodles on Sauté. Bring the broth back to a simmer on Sauté, add the noodles, and cook 6–8 min to just short of tender. They keep softening in the hot broth.
  8. Finish off the heat. Stir the chicken back in with the lemon and dill. Salt harder than feels right — soup takes more than you expect, and the noodles absorbed some.
If you are making it ahead
Cook the noodles separately and keep them out of the pot. Sitting overnight they drink the broth and go slack. Add them to each bowl as you reheat.

Storage

Fridge 4 days, freezer 3 months without the noodles. Cool in a shallow pan so it drops below 5°C fast. Reheat gently on the stove; a hard boil shreds the vegetables and toughens the chicken.

Pressure cook 12 min. Return the thighs, add the rest of the stock, bay, salt, pepper. Lid on, sealed, High Pressure, 12 min. About 12 min to reach pressure.
Release gently. Natural release 10 min, then vent the rest.
Shred. Lift the thighs out, shred with two forks, discard bones, skin, and bay leaves. Skim surface fat.
Noodles on Saute. Bring back to a simmer, add the noodles, cook 6-8 min to just short of tender.
Finish off the heat. Stir the chicken back in with lemon and dill. Salt harder than feels right.

cleanup: Cool the soup in a shallow pan and refrigerate within 2 hours; freeze portions without the noodles.
Wash the inner pot and the cutting board and forks that touched raw chicken in hot soapy water, separately from everything else.
Pull the sealing ring and wash it; wipe the lid underside and empty the condensation cup.
Wipe the counter and the tongs, and run the dishwasher if needed.

title: No-Stir Risotto
summary: Six minutes at pressure and a hard quick release gets you creamy risotto with no stirring at all. The rice-to-stock ratio is what makes or breaks it.
body:
Why this works

Stirring risotto for 20 minutes does two things: it knocks starch off the grains, and it keeps the pot at a steady simmer with the liquid absorbed evenly. A sealed pot does both for free. What you give up is control, so the numbers have to be right going in. Two of them matter: 6 minutes at high pressure, and 1 part rice to 2½ parts liquid. Push the time to 8 and you get porridge. And it must be a quick release — every extra minute under residual pressure is another minute of cooking you cannot take back.

Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 1½ cups (300g) arborio or carnaroli rice — do not rinse it
  • 3¾ cups (900ml) stock, hot
  • ½ cup (120ml) dry white wine
  • 1 large shallot or ½ onion, finely minced
  • 3 tbsp butter, divided · 1 tbsp olive oil
  • 70g Parmigiano-Reggiano, grated fine
  • 1 tsp salt · plenty of black pepper

Method

  1. Sweat the shallot. Sauté on Normal with the oil and 1 tbsp butter. Cook the shallot 3 min until soft with no color at all.
  2. Toast the rice. Add the dry rice and stir 2–3 min until the grains turn chalky-translucent at the edges and smell faintly nutty. This step is what keeps them separate instead of gluey.
  3. Deglaze with the wine. Pour it in and stir until it has nearly evaporated, scraping the base clean as you go. Toasted rice sticks, and stuck rice is a burn notice. Press Cancel.
  4. Add the stock and level it. Pour in the hot stock, stir once, and level the rice so no grains sit above the liquid. Lid on, valve sealed.
  5. Pressure cook 6 min. High Pressure, 6 min. Hot stock brings a small pot up in about 8 min. Set a real timer.
  6. Quick release immediately. Vent the moment the timer sounds — stand to the side of the valve. The pot will look soupy and slightly underdone. That is correct; do not put the lid back on.
  7. Mantecare. Off the heat, beat in the remaining 2 tbsp butter and all the cheese hard for a full minute. It goes from loose to glossy and thick as the starch emulsifies. Salt, pepper, and serve straight away.
It should ripple, not stand up
Spoon some onto a warm plate and tilt it — it should slowly spread to the edge. If it holds its shape, beat in a splash of hot stock. Risotto tightens fast, so send it out a touch looser than you want it.

Storage

Risotto does not keep well — it sets firm and reheats gummy. If you have leftovers, chill them, roll them into balls around a cube of mozzarella, crumb them, and fry: arancini are the correct answer to yesterday's risotto. Fridge 2 days.

Heat the stock in a pan or the microwave and keep it hot - cold stock adds 5 min to the come-up and dulls the rice.
Mince the shallot fine and grate the cheese before you start; from the quick release to the plate is under 5 min.
Fill the sink with hot soapy water for clean-as-you-go.
Budget your time: about ~35 min.

title: Hard-Boiled Eggs That Actually Peel
summary: The 5-5-5 method: 5 minutes at high pressure, 5 minutes natural release, 5 minutes in ice water. Steam gets under the membrane so even fresh eggs shed their shells cleanly.
body:
Why this works

Steam under pressure forces moisture between the shell membrane and the white, so the shell lifts away in sheets instead of tearing chunks out. It works on eggs you bought yesterday, which is the whole point — boiling wants week-old eggs to peel this cleanly. The pattern is 5–5–5: 5 min at high pressure, 5 min natural release, 5 min in ice water. Add about 6 min for the pot to reach pressure before the count starts.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 12 large eggs, cold from the fridge
  • 1 cup (240ml) cold water
  • Trivet or steamer basket
  • Ice and cold water for the bath — about 1 L of each

Method

  1. Load the pot. Pour in 1 cup cold water, set the trivet, stack the eggs on top. Two loose layers is fine; they do not need to sit in a single layer.
  2. Build the ice bath. Fill a large bowl with ice and cold water while the pot works. Do it now — you get about 20 seconds of slack later.
  3. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve to Sealing, High Pressure 5 min. The pot takes roughly 6 min to seal and pressurize; the 5 min only starts after that.
  4. Natural release 5 min. When it beeps, leave it completely alone for exactly 5 min. That is carryover cooking, not idle time.
  5. Quick release the rest. Move the valve to Venting, stand clear of the steam, and open as soon as the pin drops.
  6. Ice bath 5 min. Tongs the eggs straight into the ice water. The white contracts away from the shell here — skip it and they fight you.
  7. Peel. Crack the fat end where the air pocket sits, roll the egg under your palm, peel under a thin stream of cold water.
Softer yolks
Drop the pressure time and keep everything else identical: 4 min for a firm but bright center, 3 min for jammy, 2 min for barely set. The 5 min natural release and 5 min ice bath do not change.

Storage

Unpeeled, they keep 7 days in the fridge. Peeled, 3–4 days in a covered container with a damp paper towel laid over them. Do not freeze them — the whites turn rubbery.

title: Homemade Yogurt
summary: Two liters of thick yogurt from milk and two spoonfuls of starter. This is not a pressure cook - the Yogurt setting just holds 43C for eight hours, which is the one thing a stovetop cannot do unattended.
body:
Why this works

Nothing here is pressure cooked. The Yogurt button holds the pot at a steady 43°C for hours, and that is the whole trick — a stovetop cannot babysit a temperature overnight. Scalding the milk to 82°C first denatures the whey proteins so they set into a firm gel instead of a thin, weepy one; that single step is the difference between yogurt and warm milk. Not every model has a Yogurt button — the Duo and Duo Plus do, most Lux models do not. Check before you buy the milk.

Ingredients (serves 8)

  • 2 L (½ gallon) whole milk — avoid ultra-pasteurized if you can
  • 2 tbsp plain yogurt with live active cultures, or one packet of freeze-dried starter
  • Optional: 2 tbsp milk powder for a firmer set
  • An instant-read thermometer. This recipe does not work by eye.

Method

  1. Start clean. Wash and dry the inner pot, lid, and sealing ring. Stray bacteria compete with your culture and win.
  2. Scald to 82°C. Milk into the pot, press Yogurt and adjust to Boil (or run Sauté on low and stir). About 30 min for 2 L. Stir the bottom now and then so it does not scorch.
  3. Cool to 43°C. Lift the inner pot out and let it sit on the counter, about 45 min. Set the pot in a sink of ice water instead and it is 15 min. Above 46°C you kill the culture, so check with the thermometer, not your finger.
  4. Temper the starter. Whisk the 2 tbsp yogurt into a cup of the warm milk until smooth, then stir that back into the pot. Dumping cold starter straight in gives you lumps.
  5. Incubate 8 hours. Pot back in the base, lid on (valve position is irrelevant — there is no pressure), press Yogurt and set 8:00. Do not stir or peek; the gel is fragile while it forms.
  6. Chill 6 hours. Refrigerate undisturbed. It firms up considerably as it cools, so judging it warm will fool you every time.
Tart vs. thick
Longer incubation means more sour, not more firm. 8 hours is mild, 10 is noticeably tangy, 12 is sharp. For Greek-style, strain the chilled batch through cheesecloth for 2 hours — you lose about a third of the volume as whey, which is good in bread and smoothies.

Storage

Two weeks in clean jars in the fridge. Save 2 tbsp from this batch to start the next one; a strain stays reliable for roughly 5 generations before it turns sluggish and you should buy fresh starter.

title: One-Pot Mashed Potatoes
summary: Potatoes cook in 8 minutes at high pressure in a single cup of liquid, then get mashed in the same pot. No colander, no second pan, no waterlogged potatoes.
body:
Why this works

Boiled potatoes sit in two liters of water and drink some of it. Pressure-cooked potatoes cook in 1 cup of liquid that mostly turns to steam, so they come out drier and take butter and milk far better. You also mash in the pot you cooked in. Cook time is 8 min at high pressure — add about 9 min for the pot to come up and 2 min for the quick release.

Ingredients (serves 6)

  • 1.4 kg (3 lb) Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled, cut in 5cm chunks
  • 1 cup (240ml) water or chicken stock · 1 tsp salt
  • 85g butter, cut up
  • 180ml whole milk or cream, warmed
  • Salt and white pepper to finish

Method

  1. Cut them even. Peel and cut into 5cm chunks. Uneven chunks give you a mash with hard lumps in it — this is the only part of the recipe with any technique in it.
  2. Load the pot. Potatoes straight into the liquid with the salt, no trivet. They should sit in it, not swim.
  3. Warm the dairy. Heat the milk and butter together while the pot works, 60–90 sec in the microwave. Cold dairy shocks the starch and makes the mash gluey.
  4. Cook 8 min. High pressure, valve Sealing. Roughly 9 min to come up, then the 8 min count.
  5. Quick release. Valve to Venting the moment it beeps. Letting them sit in residual heat pushes them past done and into wet.
  6. Drain the excess. Tip off any standing liquid but keep a few tablespoons — that starchy liquid is your insurance if the mash goes stiff.
  7. Mash in the pot. Add the warm butter and milk and work it with a hand masher, or push it through a ricer and fold it back in. Do not reach for a stick blender; it turns potatoes into wallpaper paste in about four seconds.
  8. Season hard. Potatoes take more salt than you expect. Salt, then white pepper, then taste again before it leaves the pot.
Holding them
Press Keep Warm and rest the lid on loosely — they hold an hour without a skin forming. Stir in a splash of warm milk right before serving to loosen them back up.

Storage

4 days in the fridge. Reheat with a splash of milk over low heat, or in short microwave bursts with a stir between each. They freeze acceptably as long as there is plenty of fat in them.

title: Steamed Vegetables in Three Minutes
summary: Zero to three minutes at high pressure with an instant quick release. Pressure steam keeps the color and the bite, but the window between crisp-tender and mush is about 45 seconds, so stay at the pot.
body:
Why this works

Pressure steam hits every surface at once, so vegetables cook fast and hold their color instead of leaching it into a pot of water. The catch is the margin. At high pressure the gap between crisp-tender and army-canteen mush is roughly 45 seconds, which is why the release is instant — the vegetables keep cooking in trapped steam, and the valve is your off switch. Cook times run 0–3 min, plus about 5 min for the pot to come to pressure.

Ingredients (serves 4)

  • 700g vegetables, cut to a uniform size
  • 1 cup (240ml) cold water
  • Steamer basket or trivet — the vegetables must sit above the water, not in it
  • 1 tbsp olive oil · salt · half a lemon

Method

  1. Cut for one timing. Everything in the basket has to finish together. Broccoli and cauliflower in florets, green beans whole, carrots in 1cm coins, small potatoes quartered.
  2. Pick the time. Broccoli, cauliflower, asparagus, spinach: 0 min. Green beans, snap peas, cabbage wedges: 1 min. Carrot coins, brussels sprouts, sliced beets: 2–3 min. Zero is a real setting — the pot pressurizes and immediately stops.
  3. Load cold. 1 cup cold water in the pot, basket in, vegetables on top. Cold water gives a slower ramp and more even cooking than hot.
  4. Come to pressure. Lid on, valve Sealing, High Pressure at your chosen time. Figure about 5 min before the count starts.
  5. Release the second it beeps. Stand at the pot and move the valve to Venting immediately — not after you finish what you were doing. Thirty seconds of delay is a full doneness level.
  6. Lift the basket out. Get them out of the hot pot and onto a plate right away or the residual heat finishes the job for you.
  7. Dress while hot. Salt, olive oil, a squeeze of lemon. Seasoning sticks to hot vegetables and slides off cold ones.
If they came out soft
Drop to 0 min next time and shock the batch in ice water for 30 sec straight out of the basket. Undershooting is recoverable — put the lid back on for a minute. Overshooting is not.

Storage

4 days refrigerated. They firm back up cold and are good in salads and grain bowls. Reheating steamed vegetables a second time rarely improves them, so cook what you will eat.

title: Pot-in-Pot Cheesecake
summary: A 7-inch cheesecake steamed on a trivet in a foil sling. Sealed steam is the gentle, moist, dead-even heat cheesecake wants, and a full natural release is what keeps the top from cracking.
body:
Why this works

Cheesecake wants low, moist, even heat, which is exactly what a sealed pot full of steam is. No water bath to slosh, no oven swinging 15°C either side of the dial, no browned top. Cracks come from thermal shock, so the release is a full natural one — about 20 min — and the cake then cools slowly on the counter before it goes anywhere near the fridge. Cook time is 37 min at high pressure, plus roughly 10 min to come up.

Ingredients (serves 8)

  • 17cm (7 inch) springform pan · trivet · a foil sling
  • 120g graham cracker crumbs · 60g melted butter · 1 tbsp sugar
  • 450g full-fat cream cheese, properly at room temperature
  • 100g sugar · 1 tbsp cornstarch · 1 tsp vanilla
  • 120g sour cream · 2 large eggs, room temperature
  • 1½ cups (360ml) water for the pot

Method

  1. Bring everything to room temperature. Cream cheese and eggs out on the counter a full hour. Cold cream cheese never beats smooth and you will chase those lumps to the end.
  2. Press and chill the crust. Mix crumbs, sugar, and melted butter; press firmly into the pan base and 1cm up the sides with the flat bottom of a glass. Freeze it 10 min while the cheese softens so it sets and does not float loose.
  3. Make the batter. Beat cream cheese and sugar smooth on low, scraping down twice. Add cornstarch, vanilla, and sour cream. Then the eggs one at a time on the lowest speed — air beaten into the batter is what makes it puff and crack.
  4. Fill and cover. Pour in, rap the pan on the counter to bring bubbles up, then cover tightly with foil so condensation cannot drip onto the surface.
  5. Come to pressure. 1½ cups water and the trivet in the pot, lower the pan in on the foil sling. Lid on, valve Sealing. About 10 min to pressurize.
  6. Cook 37 min. High pressure. When it comes out the center should still wobble as one piece — it is not supposed to look baked.
  7. Full natural release. Do not touch the valve. About 20 min until the pin drops. This is the step that prevents cracks.
  8. Cool, then chill. Blot the surface dry with a paper towel, cool on the counter 1 hour, then refrigerate at least 6 hours — overnight is better. Warm it is soft and bland; cold it is a different dessert.
Sealing ring
Run a dedicated ring for desserts. A ring that has cooked curry will put curry in your cheesecake, and no amount of washing takes it back out.

Storage

5 days covered in the fridge. It freezes well: chill it fully, then wrap slices and freeze up to 2 months, thawing overnight in the fridge. Cut with a hot, dry knife and wipe the blade between slices.

title: Pressure Cook Time Chart
summary: Minutes at high pressure for 61 foods, with the release each one wants. The page to open mid-cook when you forget how long the chickpeas need.
body:
Minutes at high pressure in a 6-quart Duo at sea level. Times exclude the 10–15 min the pot takes to come to pressure and exclude the release, so budget roughly double. Cook time follows the size and thickness of each piece, not the weight in the pot — doubling a batch changes how long it takes to pressurize, not how long it cooks.

Shorthand: natural means let pressure fall on its own (20–40 min). 10 min NR means wait 10 minutes, then open the valve. quick means vent right away.

  • Kidney beans — 30 min, natural

  • Brown or green lentils — 9 min, natural
  • Red lentils (split) — 5 min, natural
  • Split peas — 10 min, natural

  • Pork shoulder, whole 3 lb — 75 min, natural

  • Shrimp, large, on trivet — 1 min, quick

Vegetables (on a trivet, 1 cup water)

  • Asparagus or green beans — 1 min, quick
  • Broccoli or cauliflower florets — 0 min, quick
  • Brussels sprouts, halved — 2 min, quick
  • Cabbage wedges — 3 min, quick
  • Carrots, 1-inch chunks — 4 min, quick
  • Corn on the cob — 2 min, quick
  • Collards or kale, chopped — 6 min, quick

  • Russets, whole 8 oz — 14 min, 5 min NR
  • Sweet potatoes, whole medium — 15 min, 5 min NR
  • Beets, whole medium — 20 min, 5 min NR
  • Butternut squash, 1-inch cubes — 4 min, quick

Eggs (on a trivet, 1 cup water, straight to an ice bath)

  • Jammy yolk — 4 min, 4 min NR then vent
  • Hard cooked — 5 min, 5 min NR then vent
  • Egg bites in a silicone mold — 9 min, 10 min NR

Stock

  • Chicken carcass stock — 45 min, natural
  • Beef bone broth — 120 min, natural
  • Shrimp shell or fish stock — 20 min, natural
  • Vegetable scrap stock — 15 min, natural

Fruit and dessert

  • Applesauce, quartered apples — 5 min, natural
