Undercook on purpose
You can always put the lid back on for 2 more minutes. You cannot un-mush a bean. With an unfamiliar food, take 15 percent off the chart and check.

title: Natural Release vs Quick Release
summary: Release is a cooking step, not a shutdown procedure. Natural keeps cooking the food as it coasts down; quick stops it cold and can wreck meat or spray starch across your ceiling.
body:
What each one physically does

Under high pressure, the liquid in the pot sits around 240°F instead of 212°F. Release is how you get back to 212°F, and the route matters.

  • Quick release: you open the valve, pressure drops in 1–3 min, and every bit of superheated liquid inside the food flashes to steam on its way out. Cooking stops almost immediately.
  • Natural release: the pot cools on its own over 20–40 min. The food stays above 212°F for a good part of that, so it keeps cooking, and the liquid stays liquid instead of erupting.

The practical consequence: natural release is worth an extra 10–20 min of gentle cooking. That is why the chart pairs long-cook foods with it — the time listed assumes the coast-down happens.

Which foods want which

  • Natural, always: beans, big cuts of meat, stock, oats, polenta, custards, anything with a lot of liquid or a lot of starch.
  • Quick, always: vegetables you want intact, seafood, eggs going to an ice bath, anything that goes from perfect to mush in 60 seconds.
  • 10 min then vent: rice, quinoa, chicken pieces, ribs, pork chops. Ten minutes lets the starch settle and the meat relax, then you stop it before it overcooks.

Why starchy things spit

Beans, grains, dal, oats, and pasta release starch and saponins into the cooking liquid, which makes it foam. Foam is liquid stiffened by bubbles, so it rides the steam straight up the valve. On quick release you get starchy water on the ceiling and, worse, a clogged valve. Natural release lets the foam collapse before anything moves.

If you must vent a foamy pot early, use short bursts: crack the valve for 2 seconds, close it, wait 10, repeat. And never fill above the half line with these foods.

Why meat seizes on a fast drop

Muscle fibers under pressure are full of hot liquid. Drop the pressure fast and that liquid boils out of the fibers as they contract, so the meat squeezes itself dry. Quick-released chicken breast is stringy and quick-released pot roast is tough — and no amount of extra cooking undoes it. Give any meat at least 10 min of natural release, and give large cuts the full drop.

The float valve is the real signal
The pot is not open until the metal pin drops flush. If it has not dropped, there is still pressure inside, no matter what the display says. Never twist the lid to test it.

Rules of thumb

  • A full natural release on a packed 6-quart pot takes 25–40 min. Plan for it or you will vent something you should not have.
  • If the recipe does not say, ask whether the food gets better or worse with 15 more minutes of heat. That answers it.
  • Natural release on a nearly empty pot is fast (10 min) because there is little hot mass to cool.

title: The Burn Notice: Why It Happens and How to Stop It
summary: The burn message means the bottom of the pot got too hot, which almost always means not enough thin liquid down there. It is fixable mid-cook and easy to prevent.
body:
What the pot is actually telling you

A temperature sensor sits under the inner pot. While liquid is boiling on the bottom, that sensor reads around 212–240°F. If the bottom goes dry or scorches, the reading spikes, the pot cuts the heat and shows Burn, Food Burn, or Ovht depending on the model. It is a scorch detector, not a smoke alarm. Your food is usually fine.

The real causes, in order of how often they happen

  1. Not enough thin liquid. One cup of water or stock, minimum. Sauce, canned tomatoes, coconut milk, and cream do not count — they are too thick to circulate and turn to steam.
  2. Fond left on the bottom after sautéing. Browned bits stuck to bare metal are the first thing to scorch. Deglaze until the spoon slides on clean steel, every time.
  3. Thick sauce stirred in. Stirring tomato sauce, barbecue sauce, or a roux through the pot puts it in contact with the bottom. Pour it on top and leave it there.
  4. Dairy or sugar in contact with the base. Milk, cream, cheese, and honey scorch at temperatures the liquid below them never reaches.
  5. Too full, or too tightly packed. A dense mass of rice or potatoes blocks convection so the bottom layer overheats while the top is cold.

Fixing it mid-cook

  1. Hit Cancel. Do not just wait it out.
  2. Quick release, keeping hands and face clear of the valve.
  3. Open the lid and lift the inner pot out with mitts. Nothing else tells you how bad it is.
  4. Scrape the bottom with a wooden or silicone spoon. If it lifts, you are fine. If it is black and welded down, transfer the good food to a bowl, wash the pot, and put it back — that layer will taste burnt through the whole dish.
  5. Add ½ to 1 cup of water or stock, stir the bottom clean, push thick ingredients to the top, and restart with the remaining time.
Do not stir it back in
The instinct is to stir and keep going. Scraped-up scorch spreads bitterness through everything. Taste the scraping before deciding.

Prevention that actually works

  • Layer, do not mix. Thin liquid on the bottom, then meat and hard vegetables, then thick sauce or tomatoes on top, unstirred. Stir only after cooking.
  • Deglaze with real volume. Half a cup of stock and 30 seconds of scraping after sautéing prevents most burn notices.
  • Rinse rice. Surface starch is glue that sticks to the base.
  • Give it room. Two-thirds full maximum, half full for starchy foods.
  • Check for a warped pot. A base that rocks on the counter has poor sensor contact and will throw false burns.

A burn notice is not a malfunction, and turning the pot off and on does not address it. If you get one twice on the same recipe, the recipe has too little thin liquid.

title: Liquid Rules and Fill Lines
summary: One cup of thin liquid minimum, two-thirds full maximum, half full for anything that foams. Pressure cooking loses almost no liquid, so stovetop volumes have to come down.
body:
The 1-cup minimum, and what it is really for

A pressure cooker needs steam, and steam has to come from somewhere. One cup of thin liquid in a 6-quart pot is the amount that reliably generates enough to pressurize and keep the bottom wet through a long cook. An 8-quart wants 1½ cups.

The word that matters is thin. Water, stock, wine, beer, thin brine, and juice all count. These do not:

  • Tomato sauce, passata, crushed tomatoes
  • Coconut milk, cream, milk, yogurt
  • Barbecue sauce, anything built on a roux
  • Condensed soup straight from the can

These are too viscous to circulate and to flash to steam. They sit on the bottom and scorch. If a recipe's only liquid is thick, add a cup of water or stock underneath it.

Liquid that arrives on its own

Meat and vegetables give up a lot of water under pressure. A pot of chicken thighs and mushrooms ends up with more liquid than you put in — a pound of mushrooms releases most of a cup, and chicken thighs release nearly as much. Start at the 1-cup minimum and let the food fill in the rest.

The fill lines

  • Two-thirds, marked inside the pot — the absolute maximum for anything. Above that there is not enough headspace for steam and the pot struggles to seal.
  • One-half — the limit for foods that foam or expand: dry beans, rice and grains, split peas and dal, oats, pasta, and applesauce. Beans roughly triple; rice roughly doubles.
  • Minimum — 1 cup thin liquid, or 1½ cups if you are cooking longer than 45 min.
Why the half line is not optional
Foam from beans and grains rides the steam into the release valve and clogs it. That is the one failure mode where the safety features have to do real work.

Cutting stovetop volumes

A sealed pot loses almost nothing to evaporation — call it a few tablespoons over an hour, against a cup or more on a stovetop simmer. So a stew that calls for 6 cups of broth over 2 hours on the stove needs about 2 to 2½ cups under pressure, and it still comes out looser than you expect. Halve the liquid in any converted braise, then reduce on Sauté at the end if the sauce is thin.

Layering order

  1. Thin liquid on the bottom, bottom scraped clean of fond.
  2. Grains, beans, or dense vegetables next.
  3. Meat above that.
  4. Thick sauce, tomatoes, dairy, or sweeteners last, poured on top and left unstirred.

The pot cooks by steam moving through the food, not by convection in liquid. Nothing needs to be submerged.

title: Pot-in-Pot Cooking
summary: Put the food in a dish, put the dish on a trivet above an inch of water, and the pot becomes a steam oven. It is how you cook two things at once and how you bake in a pressure cooker.
body:
What it is

Pot-in-pot, or PIP, means the food never touches the inner pot. Water goes in the bottom, a trivet holds a separate dish above it, and the food cooks in trapped steam at 240°F. The inner pot becomes a boiler; the dish is where dinner happens.

Why bother

  • Two things at once. Chili in the bottom, rice in a bowl on a tall trivet above it. One cycle, one pot to wash.
  • No scorching. Dairy, tomato, sugar, and thick sauces cannot burn if they are not touching the heated base. PIP is the reliable fix for a recipe that keeps throwing a burn notice.
  • Baking. Cheesecake, custard, bread pudding, dulce de leche, steamed puddings. Moist heat with no dry surface, which is exactly what those want.
  • Small batches. Two cups of rice cooks better in a bowl than spread thin across a 6-quart base.
  • Reheating. Leftovers in a bowl, 2 min, no drying out and no plastic.

Dishes that work

  • Oven-safe stainless or tempered glass bowls, 1½ to 2 quarts
  • 7-inch round cake pans and 6- or 7-inch springform pans (foil-wrap the base of a springform)
  • Ramekins, custard cups, silicone egg-bite molds
  • Wide-mouth canning jars, lids finger-tight only so pressure can equalize
  • Stackable stainless insert pans, which get you three layers in one cycle

Avoid anything not oven-safe, thin plastic, and cold glass straight from the fridge — thermal shock cracks it. Leave an inch of clearance around the dish or steam cannot circulate.

The setup

  1. Water: 1 cup for cooks under 30 min, 1½ cups for longer. It goes under the trivet and never in the dish.
  2. Trivet: the wire one that came with the pot for shallow dishes; a tall or stackable trivet if something is cooking underneath.
  3. Sling: tear a 24-inch length of foil and fold it lengthwise into a strip about 3 inches wide. Set the dish on the middle, lower it in by the ends, and fold the ends down. Lifting a hot, full dish out of a deep pot without one is how people burn their forearms.
  4. Cover the dish with foil for anything that should not get watery — cakes, custards, rice you want dry. Skip the cover if a little condensation is harmless.
Time adjustment
Heat has to cross the dish wall, so PIP runs slower. Add about 15–20 percent to the direct-pot time and use natural release. Rice is the exception: same 1:1 water, just add 2 min.

Worked combination

Curry in the base, rice above. Sauté and build the curry directly in the inner pot, leaving at least a cup of thin liquid. Set a tall trivet over it, put a bowl with 1 cup rinsed rice and 1 cup water on the trivet, and pressure cook 6 min with a 10 min natural release. Both come out done, and the rice tastes faintly of the curry steam, which is a feature.

title: Sealing Rings, Valves, and Keeping It Clean
summary: The silicone ring absorbs every smell you cook and is the part that fails. Keep two, know when to replace them, and clean the three small parts nobody looks at.
body:
The sealing ring

Silicone is porous. It takes on the smell of whatever you cook and gives it back to the next thing. Cook curry on Tuesday and your Sunday cheesecake tastes faintly of cumin. This is not a defect you can wash out.

The fix is two rings, kept separate: one for savory, one for sweet and neutral. They ship in colors for exactly this reason — red for savory, blue or clear for sweet. Store the pot with the lid inverted on top rather than locked shut, so air moves through and the ring dries.

When to replace it

Every 6 to 18 months depending on use. Replace immediately if:

  • It has stretched and no longer sits snug in the lid groove, or sags out of round
  • It has cracks, nicks, or a flattened, glazed-looking edge
  • Steam escapes around the lid rim during a cook and the pot never pressurizes
  • It smells strongly of something even after washing and airing

Rings are cheap. A ring that will not seal wastes an hour and the food in the pot.

Leak checklist before you blame the ring
Valve set to Sealing. Ring fully seated all the way around the groove. Float valve free of food. Enough thin liquid. Nothing caught on the rim. Four of five leaks are one of those.

The parts nobody cleans

  • Anti-block shield: the little metal cage under the lid beneath the steam valve. Pry it off with a firm pull. Food splatter collects underneath and a blocked shield is a genuine safety issue. Check it monthly, and always after cooking beans, oats, or anything that foams.
  • Float valve: the small metal pin that rises to lock the lid. It should drop freely when you press it. It has its own tiny silicone seal on the underside — keep that clean and seated.
  • Steam release handle: pull it straight up off the Duo lid and wash it. It comes off loose by design; that is not a broken part.
  • Condensation cup: the small plastic cup that clips to the back of the base. Empty it after every cook or it grows things.
  • Lid rim groove: lift the ring out and wipe the channel underneath. Grease collects there.

What goes in the dishwasher

  • Yes: inner pot, trivet, sealing ring, and the lid on the top rack (remove the ring and shield first)
  • Never: the base housing. It holds the heating element and the electronics. Wipe the outside and the inner rim with a damp cloth, and clean the sensor plate at the bottom of the well so nothing sits between it and the pot.

Two quick fixes

  • Deodorize: 2 cups water plus 1 cup white vinegar and a strip of lemon peel, 5 min at pressure, natural release. Then air the ring for a day.
  • Rainbow stains on the inner pot: harmless mineral discoloration, not damage. Wipe with a little vinegar.

title: Converting a Stovetop Recipe to Pressure
summary: Roughly one third of the simmer time, half the liquid, brown first on Saute, and add dairy and delicate vegetables at the end. Anything that wants crisp or reduction does not convert.
body:
The arithmetic

A stovetop simmer runs at 212°F. An Instant Pot at high pressure runs around 240°F, and reaction rates roughly double for every 18°F, so pressure cooking is about three times faster once you are up to pressure.

  • Time: take one third of the stovetop simmer time and round down. Do not count browning, prep, or the come-to-pressure time.
  • Liquid: cut it by half to two thirds, never below 1 cup of thin liquid. A sealed pot barely evaporates, so whatever you put in is still there at the end.
  • Quantity: does not change the time. A double batch cooks for the same minutes and just takes longer to pressurize.

Verify against the time chart. If your arithmetic says 12 min for beef cubes and the chart says 35, trust the chart.

Order of operations

  1. Sauté first. Brown meat in batches with space between the pieces, soften aromatics, bloom spices and tomato paste. Nothing browns once the lid is on, so this is the only flavor you will get.
  2. Deglaze completely. Wine or stock, scrape until the bottom is bare metal. Skipping this is the most common cause of a burn notice.
  3. Add the long-cook ingredients and the reduced liquid. Thick sauce and tomatoes go on top, unstirred.
  4. Pressure cook, release per the chart.
  5. Finish on Sauté. Reduce the sauce, stir in a slurry, add anything delicate.

What goes in after the lid comes off

  • Dairy of any kind — cream, milk, yogurt, cheese, coconut milk. Under pressure it curdles or scorches.
  • Peas, spinach, zucchini, and anything else that cooks in under 5 min
  • Fresh herbs, citrus juice and zest, vinegar
  • Cornstarch or flour slurries, which only thicken at a boil with the lid off
  • Pasta, unless you want it soft

What never converts

Anything whose point is a dry surface or a reduced sauce: roast chicken with crisp skin, seared steak, a ragu that gets its body from three hours of open evaporation. Also stir-fries, which are faster in a skillet, and delicate fish, which goes from raw to chalky within a minute.

The tell
If the recipe's technique is water leaving the pot, pressure is the wrong tool. If the technique is collagen and starch breaking down in liquid, it is the right one.

Worked example: beef stew

Original: brown 2 lb chuck, add 6 cups broth, simmer 2 hours, add potatoes and carrots for the last 30 min.

  1. Brown the chuck on Sauté in two batches. Soften onion, add tomato paste, cook it dark.
  2. Deglaze with ½ cup wine, scrape clean.
  3. Add the beef and 2½ cups broth — not 6. Two hours divided by three is 40 min; the chart says 35 for 2-inch cubes, so use 35.
  4. Cook 35 min, full natural release. Vegetables added now would be baby food, so they were left out.
  5. Open, add potatoes and carrots in large chunks, cook 4 min more, quick release.
  6. Thicken on Sauté with a slurry. Total: about 75 min, against 2½ hours.

title: Pressure Safety and High-Altitude Adjustments
summary: Modern electric pressure cookers cannot be opened under pressure, so the exploding-cooker stories do not apply. Steam is the actual hazard. Above 2,000 ft, add 5 percent cook time per 1,000 ft.
body:
Why the old stories do not apply

The exploding-pressure-cooker story your relatives tell comes from mid-century stovetop cookers: a single jiggler weight over a single hole, no interlock, and a lid you could twist off while the pot was still under pressure. Clog the hole or force the lid and things went badly.

An Instant Pot Duo has around ten independent safety mechanisms. The ones that matter day to day:

  • Lid interlock. The float valve rises with pressure and physically blocks the lid from turning. You cannot open a pressurized pot, however hard you try.
  • Heat cuts on an unsealed lid. If the lid is not locked, it will not start a pressure program.
  • Anti-block shield over the steam intake, so a bean skin cannot plug the release path.
  • Automatic pressure and temperature control, plus a safety valve and a thermal fuse behind that.
  • Last-resort gasket release: if everything else failed, the sealing ring extrudes through a slot in the lid and vents sideways rather than letting the lid fly.

The rules that still matter

  • Never force the lid. If it will not turn, there is pressure inside. Wait. Removing the sealing ring to free a stuck lid is genuinely dangerous.
  • Keep the valve and shield clear. Never drape a towel over the steam release, never set anything on top of it, and check the anti-block shield after cooking foamy foods.
  • Respect the fill lines. Two thirds maximum, half for foaming foods.
  • Never deep-fry under pressure, and do not use the pot for pressure canning low-acid foods — no electric multicooker is validated for it, whatever the marketing says.
  • Watch what is above the counter. A release jet aimed at a cabinet will lift the finish off it.
Steam is the real hazard
The jet leaving that valve is about 240°F and carries far more energy than boiling water. Turn the valve with the handle of a long spoon, from the side, never with a bare hand over the top, and keep your face away.

Altitude

Lower atmospheric pressure means the absolute pressure inside is lower, so the boiling point inside is lower, so food cooks slower. The rule: above 2,000 ft, add 5 percent to the cook time for every 1,000 ft of elevation. Below 2,000 ft, change nothing.

Worked example, Denver at 5,280 ft: 5,280 minus 2,000 is 3,280 ft, which is 3.28 thousands, times 5 percent, so add about 16 percent.

  • A 30 min pot roast step becomes 35 min
  • Chickpeas at 40 min become 46 min
  • Hard-cooked eggs at 5 min become 6 min

Round up to the nearest minute. Short cooks barely move; long ones move a lot, so an hour of bone broth gains ten minutes. Come-to-pressure and release times stretch at altitude too. If food comes out consistently underdone, add another 5 percent rather than assuming the pot is faulty.
